name: Gaddang
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 14 other works consulted do not discuss stress. 3 further first-hand descriptions conflict (see the conflicting-description items); the entry follows Galang 1935.
catalog_citation: Galang, Ricardo E. 1935. Ethnographic study of the Yogads of Isabela. Philippine Journal of Science 56(1):81-90, plates 1-3. Manila: Bureau of Science.
catalog_locator: journal pp. 89-90, section 'Dialect' / 'Lexical comparison'; Gaddang column of the comparative table pp. 88-89
catalog_quote: From the common terms mentioned above, it is evident that the Yogad dialect closely resembles Ibanag and Gaddang. In Yogad and Ibanag the accent appears frequently on the second syllable of the word. For example: moon bulán vulán, star bitún bitún, head ulú ulú, heart futú futú, root gammút gammú-t, four appát appá-t, seven pitú pitú. [...] In the Gaddang dialect the accent frequently appears on the first syllable of the word. For example: fire áfuy, man tólay, child ának, head úlu, eye máta, leg úffu, nail cúcu, dog átu, fish síra, bridge tétay, sickness táquit, one táta, two ádua, seven pítu, one hundred tátut. It is evident that the Yogad and Ibanag dialects have the same intonation in speaking, while that of the Gaddang is different.

new_statements.quote: 1.4. Primary stress is not predictable in terms of any phonological feature.(10) When words are spoken in isolation, primary stress may move from syllable to syllable; the position of primary stress is therefore determined by examining words in a larger context. Examples: mətákaw 'will steal', mattakáw 'will borrow', palátaŋ 'jaw bone', matarabáfo 'will work'. A secondary stress occurs on the first syllable of four or five syllable words, and since always predictable, it is non-phonemic. [...] (10) Primary stress occurs more frequently on the penult.
new_statements.citation: Troyer, Madeline. 1959. Gaddang phonology. Philippine Journal of Science 88(1):95-102.
new_statements.locator: p. 98, section 1.4 'STRESS' and footnote 10 (p. 104 of the archive.org issue scan); supporting: p. 95 (stress listed as a phoneme class), p. 99 sec. 3.1 (word defined by single primary stress), p. 101 sec. 4(3) (orthography marks stress only to disambiguate)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is phonemic (lexically contrastive, e.g. mətákaw 'will steal' vs mattakáw 'will borrow'); it falls on the penult or the final syllable, more often the penult, and cannot be predicted from segmental shape. Each phonological word (1-5 syllables) has exactly one primary stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Non-phonemic secondary stress on the first syllable of four- and five-syllable words (e.g. [mábbalafíŋgan] 'will become numb', [ʔálifámbaŋ] 'butterfly').
new_statements.exceptions: In isolation (citation forms) primary stress 'may move from syllable to syllable', so stress position must be established from words in context; practical orthography marks stress only where two words would otherwise be identical. Reid 1971 reprints this phonology with 'Stress not indicated' on the word list.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word (defined p. 99 as 1-5 syllables with a single primary stress, pronounceable in isolation); phrase/sentence intonation explicitly not studied. On the identity of the variety: the description is based on a speaker from Butigui, eastern Bontoc (now Paracelis, Mountain Province), the upland 'pagan Gaddang' who call themselves Gàdang [Gaʔdang] -- i.e. Ga'dang, Glottolog gada1258 / ISO gdg, the sister language of lowland Gaddang gadd1244. Glottolog itself files Troyer 1959 under gada1258.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted source (Troyer 1959), which the earlier scan named for gadd1244 and which Reid 1971 reprints as 'Gaddang (Gad.)', actually describes the UPLAND 'pagan Gaddang' of Butigui, eastern Bontoc (now Paracelis, Mountain Province) -- self-name Gàdang = Gaʔdang, i.e. Ga'dang, Glottolog gada1258 / ISO gdg; Glottolog files Troyer 1959 under gada1258, not gadd1244. The statement is therefore a first-hand, open, saved catalog candidate for gada1258 (whose own scan classification was no source found), and only nearest-sister evidence for lowland Gaddang gadd1244 (Nueva Vizcaya/Isabela). The one accessible first-hand lowland-Gaddang source (Yamada 1972, Bagabag) is silent on stress and marks none.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Impressionistic tendency statement: in (lowland) Gaddang the accent 'frequently' falls on the first syllable of the word -- all 15 illustrative words are disyllables, so = penult (áfuy, tólay, ának, úlu, máta..), contrasted with Yogad/Ibanag where accent is 'frequently' on the second (final) syllable of the same etyma. No claim that accent is fixed or predictable; the author's own comparative table also marks final accent on some Gaddang words (tallú 'three', annám 'six') beside penult (bálay, dánum, gámut, tafúlu, aduáfulu, tátut). Best summarized as penult-leaning word accent, contrastiveness not addressed.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated; table shows final-accented tallú, annám and many unmarked items (langit, bulan, bitun, tolay in the table vs tólay in the example list)
new_statements.identity_note: An ethnography of the Yogad (yoga1241) whose DIALECT section compares Yogad, Ibanag and 'Gaddang'; Galang's Gaddang are explicitly 'the Christian Gaddangs living in Magat River Valley' (Isabela/Nueva Vizcaya), i.e. lowland Gaddang gadd1244, observed during his 1931 Bureau of Science fieldwork in Isabela and Nueva Vizcaya -- not the upland 'pagan Gaddang'/Ga'dang (gada1258) of Troyer 1959. The comparative word table is taken 'from the work of Otto Scheerer' (Batan dialect, 1908) but carries Galang's accent marks; the accent paragraph and its 15 examples are his own. | Typological table entry 'Gaddang' with no variety, location or source given. Cannot be pinned to gadd1244.

new_statements.quote: (2) Since there are other Philippine languages that do not reflect PPH accent, e.g. Kuyonon and Tausug within Bisayan (Zorc 1977), Buhid within South Mangyan, Gaddang within Banagic, etc., it is therefore plausible that Png independently lost contrastive accent in cognate forms. (3) The development of contrastive accent could have been a dialectal feature of PPH, and languages like Ivatan, Tausug, Pangasinan, and Gaddang are all survivors of dialects in which such contrasts were not made, while Ilokano, Ibanag, Ifugao, Tagalog, and Hanunoo are all survivors of dialects where contrasts were made.

new_statements.quote: Ito ang pares minimal na nagpapatunay ng mahabang patinig (vowel length) at diin (stress): ... Diin (stress) [Ɂɑ.ˈri] arí 'haligi' [ˈɁɑ.ri] ári 'alis' [Ɂɑp.ˈpɑn] appán 'kunin' [ˈɁɑp.pɑn]/[ˈɁɑ.pɑn] sa Santiago áppan 'pain' [bi.ˈlɑng] biláng 'numero' [ˈbi.lɑng] bílang 'bilang' || 7.2 Pahilis: Lagyan ng tuldik pahilís (´) ang mga salita na may kapareha ng baybay pero magkaiba ang diin. Isulat ang pahilis (´) sa itaas ng patinig ng pantig na may diin. Halimbawa: [ˈdu.lang] dúlang 'mababang mesa' [du.ˈlang] duláng 'tulala' [ˈba.lu] bálu 'balo' [ba.ˈlu] balú 'pinipig' ...
new_statements.translation: These are the minimal pairs that prove long vowels (vowel length) and stress: ... Stress: arí 'post' vs ári 'leave'; appán 'get' vs áppan (ápan in Santiago) 'bait'; biláng 'number' vs bílang 'as'. || 7.2 Acute: Put the acute accent on words that have a same-spelled partner but differ in stress. Write the acute over the vowel of the stressed syllable. Examples: dúlang 'low table' vs duláng 'dazed'; bálu 'widow' vs balú 'pounded young rice' ...
new_statements.citation: Kagawaran ng Edukasyon (Dibisyon ng Nueva Vizcaya, Dibisyon ng Isabela, Dibisyon ng Lungsod Cauayan, Dibisyon ng Lungsod Santiago), Translators Association of the Philippines, Inc. & Komisyon sa Wikang Filipino. 2019 [web PDF posted 2024]. Ortografíya na Gaddang / Ortograpiyang Gaddang. Maynila: Komisyon sa Wikang Filipino. 100 pp. ISBN 978-621-8064-87-4. (KWF 'Mga Ortograpiya' series; bilingual Gaddang / Filipino.)
new_statements.locator: p.27 (printed p.24, Filipino column of sec. 1.x 'pares minimal') and p.59 (printed p.56, sec. 7.2 'Pahilis'); Gaddang-language versions on the facing pages PDF 26 and 58
new_statements.relation_note: States that both vowel length (dōn 'leaf' vs don; māt 'river' vs mat; kūn vs kun; būk vs buk; written with a macron 'pahaba/pasoddag') and stress ('diin', written with the acute 'pahilís/patummad' only on same-spelled pairs) are contrastive, giving penult-vs-final stress minimal pairs (ári/arí, áppan/appán, bílang/biláng, dúlang/duláng, bálu/balú); stressed syllables closed by glottal stop take the circumflex (pakupyâ; 'used for Paracelis words'). No default-position rule is given; stress is treated as a lexical property to be marked where distinctive.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is lexically contrastive (penult vs final minimal pairs) and independent of a separate vowel-length contrast; the orthography marks stress with an acute only where a homograph exists.
new_statements.exceptions: dialect variants: Santiago ápan for áppan; pakupyâ forms characteristic of Paracelis; loanword syllabification notes (5.1-5.4) mention where 'diin' falls in Spanish loans (e.g. ekonomIYA)
new_statements.identity_note: Orthography written by Gaddang teachers and elders from Nueva Vizcaya (Bayombong, Bagabag, Solano..), Isabela (Santiago, Cauayan) and Paracelis with the TAP Gaddang New Testament translators; the core is lowland (Christian) Gaddang [gad]; Paracelis Ga'dang (gada1258) is treated as a dialect and gets separate notes (pakupya 'Magagamit ito sa mga salita ng Paracelis'), and a Santiago variant is flagged in the stress pairs ('áppan/ápan sa Santiago') [name in source: Gaddang (Nueva Vizcaya, Isabela incl. Santiago and Cauayan; also Paracelis, Mountain Province); pages printed p.23 (Gaddang) / p.24 (Filipino) = pp.26-27, sec. 1 'Grafema na Gaddang', minimal pairs; printed p.55-56 = pp.58-59, sec. 7 'Mga Tuldik', 7.1 Pahaba, 7.2 Pahilis; p.17 table of diacritics]

new_statements.relation_note: The study elicited 50 Gaddang words (27 'common', 23 'not common') from Bagabag informants and classified each by part of speech and by 'Pronunciation (Stress)', i.e. which syllable (counted from the beginning of the word) the informants stressed. Tables 3-4 give sample entries with ad hoc stress marks (Afak/Afac; Di’osMab’balat; Fu’tuk; Kap’pakel; Payàw; Attung at Alo; Bal’ya’wan; Karangàt; Maca’pang’ua; Pàtta). Table 5 totals: 1st syllable 27 (54 %), 2nd 15 (30 %), 3rd 4 (8 %), 'undifferentiated' 4 (8 %; interjections/phrases). The authors conclude that the majority of the words are stressed on the first syllable and (abstract) that 'some of these words are stressed in accordance to their…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule is stated. Of 50 informant-chosen Bagabag Gaddang words the authors judge 54 % stressed on the first syllable, 30 % on the second, 8 % on the third and 8 % 'undifferentiated'; they summarise this as 'majority stressed on the first syllable'. Their own sample forms show both non-final (Pàtta, Fu’tuk, Kap’pakel) and final (Payàw, Karangàt) stress.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Undifferentiated' items (4/50) are interjections/phrases such as 'Dios Mabbalat'; stress said to follow 'morphologic functions' or 'emotions conveyed' for some words (abstract), without examples of the conditioning.
new_statements.identity_note: Key informants 'are all residents of Bagabag, Nueva Vizcaya, all are members and some are officers of the Nueva Vizcaya's National Coalition of Indigenous People (Gaddang Tribe)', ages 30-75; the introduction places the group in Bayombong, Solano, Bagabag = Christianized lowland Gaddang, gadd1244 (same town as Wolfenden 1954, Yamada 1972 and McFarland's GAD-B point); not upland Ga'dang gada1258. Authors are educators, not linguists; the journal is an OMICS-family open-access title (no DOI printed).

sources.quote: 1.4. Primary stress is not predictable in terms of any phonological feature.(10) When words are spoken in isolation, primary stress may move from syllable to syllable; the position of primary stress is therefore determined by examining words in a larger context. Examples: mətákaw 'will steal', mattakáw 'will borrow', palátaŋ 'jaw bone', matarabáfo 'will work'. A secondary stress occurs on the first syllable of four or five syllable words, and since always predictable, it is non-phonemic. [...] (10) Primary stress occurs more frequently on the penult.
sources.locator: p. 98, section 1.4 'STRESS' and footnote 10 (p. 104 of the archive.org issue scan); supporting: p. 95 (stress listed as a phoneme class), p. 99 sec. 3.1 (word defined by single primary stress), p. 101 sec. 4(3) (orthography marks stress only to disambiguate)
sources.note: Stress is a phoneme class; sec. 1.4 (p.98): primary stress is not predictable from any phonological feature (mətákaw 'will steal' vs mattakáw 'will borrow'); fn.10: primary stress occurs more frequently on the penult; secondary stress predictable on first syllable of 4-5 syllable words; word = 1-5 syllables with one primary stress. BUT informant is from Butigui, Bontoc (Paracelis, Mountain Province) = upland 'pagan Gaddang' = Ga'dang, Glottolog gada1258.

sources.quote: Ito ang pares minimal na nagpapatunay ng mahabang patinig (vowel length) at diin (stress): ... Diin (stress) [Ɂɑ.ˈri] arí 'haligi' [ˈɁɑ.ri] ári 'alis' [Ɂɑp.ˈpɑn] appán 'kunin' [ˈɁɑp.pɑn]/[ˈɁɑ.pɑn] sa Santiago áppan 'pain' [bi.ˈlɑng] biláng 'numero' [ˈbi.lɑng] bílang 'bilang' || 7.2 Pahilis: Lagyan ng tuldik pahilís (´) ang mga salita na may kapareha ng baybay pero magkaiba ang diin. Isulat ang pahilis (´) sa itaas ng patinig ng pantig na may diin. Halimbawa: [ˈdu.lang] dúlang 'mababang mesa' [du.ˈlang] duláng 'tulala' [ˈba.lu] bálu 'balo' [ba.ˈlu] balú 'pinipig' ...
sources.locator: p.27 (printed p.24, Filipino column of sec. 1.x 'pares minimal') and p.59 (printed p.56, sec. 7.2 'Pahilis'); Gaddang-language versions on the facing pages PDF 26 and 58
sources.note: States that both vowel length (dōn 'leaf' vs don; māt 'river' vs mat; kūn vs kun; būk vs buk; written with a macron 'pahaba/pasoddag') and stress ('diin', written with the acute 'pahilís/patummad' only on same-spelled pairs) are contrastive, giving penult-vs-final stress minimal pairs (ári/arí, áppan/appán, bílang/biláng, dúlang/duláng, bálu/balú); stressed syllables closed by glottal stop take the circumflex (pakupyâ; 'used for Paracelis words'). No default-position rule is given; stress is treated as a lexical property to be marked where distinctive.

sources.citation: Zorc, R. David. 1979. On the development of contrastive word accent: Pangasinan, a case in point. In Nguyen Dang Liem (ed.), South-East Asian Linguistic Studies, vol. 3, 241-258. Pacific Linguistics C-45. Canberra: Australian National University.
sources.quote: (2) Since there are other Philippine languages that do not reflect PPH accent, e.g. Kuyonon and Tausug within Bisayan (Zorc 1977), Buhid within South Mangyan, Gaddang within Banagic, etc., it is therefore plausible that Png independently lost contrastive accent in cognate forms. (3) The development of contrastive accent could have been a dialectal feature of PPH, and languages like Ivatan, Tausug, Pangasinan, and Gaddang are all survivors of dialects in which such contrasts were not made, while Ilokano, Ibanag, Ifugao, Tagalog, and Hanunoo are all survivors of dialects where contrasts were made.
sources.locator: pp. 243-244, section 2 'The position of Pangasinan' (pp. 3-4 of); tree on p. 244 puts Gaddang with Ibanag and Isneg in Northern Cordilleran 'Banagic'
sources.note: Framework: PPH word accent = contrastive penult vowel length; Pangasinan, Casiguran Dumagat (partly Ibanag) lost it and re-developed length secondarily.

sources.quote: From the common terms mentioned above, it is evident that the Yogad dialect closely resembles Ibanag and Gaddang. In Yogad and Ibanag the accent appears frequently on the second syllable of the word. For example: moon bulán vulán, star bitún bitún, head ulú ulú, heart futú futú, root gammút gammú-t, four appát appá-t, seven pitú pitú. [...] In the Gaddang dialect the accent frequently appears on the first syllable of the word. For example: fire áfuy, man tólay, child ának, head úlu, eye máta, leg úffu, nail cúcu, dog átu, fish síra, bridge tétay, sickness táquit, one táta, two ádua, seven pítu, one hundred tátut. It is evident that the Yogad and Ibanag dialects have the same intonation in speaking, while that of the Gaddang is different.
sources.locator: journal pp. 89-90, section 'Dialect' / 'Lexical comparison' (pp. 109-110 of the archive.org whole-issue scan); Gaddang column of the comparative table pp. 88-89
sources.note: Also notes Gaddang shares f (< *p before u) with Ibanag/Yogad; 'The Yogads have a peculiar intonation in speaking'.
